Samir - thanks again for taking the time earlier. Quick recap and proposed next steps from today's discovery:

Call recap (what I heard):
- Primary SLO: p95 generation latency <= 150ms for our most common prompt (avg prompt length 120 tokens). p99 target discussed at 300ms for critical flows.
- Throughput: baseline ~120 req/s, expected peak bursts up to 300 req/s during settlement windows.
- Concurrency: up to 400 concurrent sessions across a geo; typical steady-state ~80-120.
- Streaming: yes - customers rely on partial token streaming for UX; want latency-to-first-token <= 80ms.
- Failure tolerance: queueing allowed for short bursts (queue time < 10s), but need graceful fallback to smaller model for sustained overloads.

Autoscale specifics you asked about:
- Warm pool / pre-warmed instances to handle short bursts.
- Scale-up time expectations and how queueing is handled during scale events.
- How we recommend sizing warm pools vs burst capacity.

Attachments: I'm attaching two files:
- fastpay_slo_matrix.xlsx (SLO matrix template)
- redwood_autoscale_playbook.pdf (how our autoscale/warm pool works + recommended tests)

2) Schedule a technical deep-dive between your infra/ops and Rishi to run through scale numbers and any network/KMS constraints. Rishi - can you propose 30/60/90-minute slots for early next week?
3) We'll propose a short soak/load window (we recommend a 30-60 minute ramp to peak) and can run a joint test using our staging infra.

Samir / team - quick tech notes to address your questions:

1) Cold-start / scale-up times:
- For warm-starting a new preemptible worker with our optimized runtime on an A100, cold-start (container + model load) is typically 60-90s if the model is not cached. With pre-warmed VMs and model cached in memory (warm pool), it's sub-5s to accept traffic.
- For L4-equivalent smaller instances (quantized models), cold-start can be ~30-60s; warm pool acceptance is ~2-4s.

2) Warm pool sizing guidance:
- Rule-of-thumb: 1 pre-warmed A100 worker per ~80-120 concurrent streaming sessions (depends on model and sequence length). For non-streaming generation, 1 worker can handle more batched throughput.
- For bursty traffic (peaks ~2-3x baseline), we recommend a combination: a small warm pool sized for ~30-40% of expected peak and the ability to burst via queued requests and cold-started instances for the remaining.

3) Streaming latency-to-first-token:
- Our measurement for the 80ms target is runtime-to-network egress under ideal network conditions. Real-world client-to-first-token includes client-side networking (CDN/proxy) and downstream latency - add ~20-50ms depending on region. We can instrument end-to-end tests during the trial.

4) Queueing behavior / SLOs:
- We support short front-end queueing with prioritized lanes. Default behavior: if pre-warmed capacity is exhausted, requests enter a short queue (~10s default) while we spin additional workers. If queue > threshold or wait > configured limit, we can automatically route to a smaller, compatible model variant to keep user-visible latency acceptable.

5) Testing suggestion:
- Recommend a 30-60 minute ramp to peak with telemetry: p50/p95/p99, latency-to-first-token, queue depth, and error rates. We'll provide a runbook and helper scripts from the playbook I attached.

Happy to walk through specifics on a call - I can demo warm pool behavior and queue handling if helpful.
